readerTitle: The couple who asked for the price first
caseNote: 가상 사례 (호텔 그룹 내 웨딩 세일즈팀, 포장 박스 제조 공장) · 적용 레슨: 자격 확인 + 탐색 질문
insight: "얼마예요?"라는 첫 질문에 바로 가격으로 답하지 않는다. 몇 가지 질문으로 맞는 고객인지 확인하고(자격 확인), 고객 자신의 말로 필요를 찾은 뒤(탐색 질문) 제안한다.
misconception: 고객이 가격을 물으면 바로 가격표를 주는 것이 친절하고 빠른 판매다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 SAL-01-04(Qualifying), SAL-01-05(Discovery)를 적용한 레슨
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 인물, 호텔, 공장, 수량은 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다.
관련 레슨 SAL-01-04, SAL-01-05의 개념 정의와 용어(qualifying, discovery)가 본 레슨 표현과 일치하는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: The couple who asked for the price first
body: Maya sells weddings for a city hotel that belongs to a large hotel group. Her team has three packages, a price sheet and a monthly target.
On Saturday, a couple walks in, sits down and asks one thing: "How much is your wedding package?" The easy move is to slide the price sheet across the table. Maya doesn't, yet.

image.label: A couple at a hotel sales desk with a price sheet on the table
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 호텔 라운지의 상담 테이블, 예비 부부가 앉아 있고 맞은편 직원 앞에 뒤집힌 가격표 한 장. 실제 호텔 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya do first?
body: The couple seems keen, but she knows nothing about them yet. Her ballroom holds 180 guests, and most Saturdays next year are already booked.

options.text: Hand over the price sheet. They asked, so answer.
options.feedback: It's honest and fast, but they may compare totals and leave before learning whether a package fits their date, guest list or budget at all.

options.text: Ask a few quick questions: date, guest count, rough budget, who else decides
options.feedback: This is **qualifying**: checking whether this is a sale you can actually make before spending an hour on it. A price makes more sense once you know which package it's for.

options.text: Offer 10% off if they book today
options.feedback: Pressure might lock in a date, but you give away money before you know if they even fit. A rushed yes also tends to become a cancellation.

cards.title: Four questions, two minutes.
body: Maya asks lightly, as part of the conversation:
list: **Date:** a Saturday next October. Two are still open.
**Budget:** they name a range near her middle package.
**Who decides:** both sets of parents are helping pay, so they'll want a say.
cards.callout: It's a real prospect. And now Maya knows to invite the parents to the next meeting.

cards.title: "We just want it to feel relaxed."
body: The couple qualifies. Then they add that they want the day to feel relaxed, not stiff. Maya has an hour. What does she do with it?

options.text: Show the premium package. Live music and a lounge feel relaxed.
options.feedback: It might impress, but it's Maya's idea of relaxed, not theirs. Guessing often sells the wrong thing or the right thing at a price that scares them off.

options.text: Ask what relaxed means to them, and what bothered them at weddings they've been to
options.feedback: This is **discovery**: asking open questions until the customer describes the problem in their own words. Their answer will shape the package better than any brochure.

options.text: Give them a tour and let the rooms speak for themselves
options.feedback: A tour builds excitement, but without questions Maya learns little. Better to ask first, then tour the rooms that match what she heard.

cards.title: Relaxed meant three specific things.
body: Their answers were concrete. One grandmother uses a wheelchair. Half the guests fly in from abroad. And at a friend's wedding, a four-hour seated dinner left everyone exhausted.

So Maya proposes the middle package with changes: the ground-floor terrace instead of the upstairs ballroom, a block of rooms for travelling guests, and a shorter dinner followed by open seating. She repeats their words back as she explains each change. The parents, invited to the next meeting, hear the same reasons.

image.label: Three customer worries linked to three package changes
image.brief: 왼쪽에 고객이 말한 세 가지(휠체어 이용 할머니, 해외에서 오는 하객, 너무 긴 저녁 식사), 오른쪽에 대응하는 제안(1층 테라스, 객실 블록, 짧은 코스와 자유 좌석)을 화살표로 연결한 인포그래픽. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Questions can go wrong too.
body: Qualifying is not a test the customer must pass. A couple with half the budget might fit a Friday or a winter date. Ruling them out too fast loses a sale you could have made.

Discovery fails when it feels like an interrogation, or when you ask questions and then pitch the same package anyway. Customers notice. Ask fewer questions, and **let the answers change your offer**.

cards.title: Now it's a box factory.
body: You sell for a factory that makes printed shipping boxes. An email arrives from a candle brand: "Price for 20,000 custom boxes, needed in five weeks?" Your schedule is tight that month.

options.text: Send your standard quote within the hour
options.feedback: Speed looks good, but you don't know if five weeks fits your production schedule, or why they need these boxes. You may quote the wrong box or a date you can't meet.

options.text: Call to confirm the deadline, who approves, and what the boxes must do
options.feedback: The deadline and approver are **qualifying**. Asking what the boxes must do is **discovery**. If candles are breaking in transit, the sale is about protection, not just print.

options.text: Decline. The schedule is too tight.
options.feedback: Safe for capacity, but you skip the question that matters. They might accept a split delivery, or the date might not be as fixed as the email suggests.

cards.softwareNote: The same pattern applies when a demo request arrives at a software company. Check team size, timing and who signs before the demo. Then ask what they use today and what keeps breaking, before showing a single feature.

cards.title: Answer "how much?" with a few good questions first.
body: This lesson used two ideas from the unit. **Qualifying** checked that the date, size, budget and decision-makers fit. **Discovery** turned a vague wish into specific needs the offer could meet.
**Try it today:** write down the four questions that would tell you, in two minutes, whether a new inquiry is a real fit for your business.
